If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
The method `MathUtils.equals(double[], double[])` from the Apache Commons Math library compares two arrays of `double` values element-wise. It checks if the arrays are of equal length and then iterates over each element to compare them using another method `MathUtils.equals(double, double)`.

Looking at the failing test case `testArrayEquals()`, it tests the behavior of the `equals` method when both arrays have a single element which is `Double.NaN`. The test asserts that `MathUtils.equals(new double[] { Double.NaN }, new double[] { Double.NaN })` should return `false`.

The current bug report mentions that there is a concern that the `equals` method in `MathUtils` returns true when both arguments are `NaN`, which might contradict the IEEE standard.

Based on the implementation of the `MathUtils.equals(double[], double[])` method, if both `x[i]` and `y[i]` are `Double.NaN`, the method will return `true` because of how `Double.NaN` is handled in Java. This behavior is consistent with the issue reported. 

To fix this issue and align with the IEEE standard, the `equals` method should be updated to handle `NaN` values differently, possibly by explicitly checking for `Double.NaN` values and returning `false` if encountered.

Next, I will provide the best location to fix this issue in the code.
```java
org.apache.commons.math.util.MathUtils.equals(double[], double[])
```

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
